By: Joy Summers | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Can Pravin's prescription save South Africa

Summary:
All eyes are on the finance minister as ratings agencies threaten downgrades and as rising interest rates put further pressure on citizens

Further information:
On the Edge of Junk

Wednesday’s budget speech will be one of the most critical since the advent of democracy in 1994.
Finance Minister Pravin Gordhan will present his spending plan, expected to be R1.45 trillion, for 2016 just over two months after President Jacob Zuma fired Nhlanhla Nene, which shocked the country and investors, and replaced him with little-known ANC MP David “Des” van Rooyen.
The move knocked the rand to an all-time low and JSE stocks lost tens of billions of rands in value. Days later, in an effort to restore confidence, President Zuma reappointed Gordhan to the job.
As Gordhan steps up to the podium, for his first budget since 2014, and says “Madam Speaker” in Parliament, he will know that he needs to address a number of tough challenges.
These include international ratings agencies breathing down his neck with the possibility of a downgrade to junk status, an economy on the brink of recession, declining tax revenues, high unemployment, rising interest rates, falling commodity prices, a devastating drought and looming municipal polls.
To balance the government books, Gordhan is expected to limit or cut expenditure and hike tax rates.
Nedbank economists Nicky Weimar, Dennis Dykes and Isaac Matshego said this week: “Gordhan has the unenviable task of producing a budget in exceedingly tough economic times that will convincingly illustrate government’s determination to restore fiscal discipline to avoid a further downgrade of South Africa’s sovereign risk rating to speculative status, and restore public and investor trust in National Treasury after the confidence-sapping events of December last year.”
Peter Montalto, a London-based economist for Nomura, said: “We expect a mixture of tax increases and expenditure cuts to offset higher spending on education and debt service costs, as well as the marked impact of lower growth on revenues.”
The country got its first investment grade rating from Moody’s Investors Service in May 1995. Now, almost 21 years later, that status is at risk.

Press Release:


Banking on Gordhan
This week, ratings agencies took out their notebooks as Finance Minister Pravin Gordhan delivered the most anticipated budget speech in South Africa’s democratic history. Calling for reforms, an end to corruption, wasteful expenditure and state-owned entity bail-outs, will his plans to ignite economic growth and deal harshly with inefficiencies manage to reverse the tightening noose of a looming junk status rating? Carte Blanche weighs in on Budget 2016.


Script:


ON THE EDGE OF JUNK: FINAL SCRIPT TX SUNDAY 28th Feb 2016


Commentary one dur: 9.5
9/12- The day President Zuma announced that unknown MP, Des Van Rooyen would replace finance minister Nhlanla Nene

Zuma up sound
I have decided to remove Mr. Nhlanhle Nene as minister of finance…

Commentary Two 10sec
That decision set off a market bloodbath. The rand nosedived, as some suggested this was an attempt by the President to capture the treasury.

LINK
A lot has happened since then, millions were wiped out of our savings, the president has lost political capital, and SA finds itself on the edge of junk status

Commentary Three 15.5 sec
Forced by markets and some cool heads, the president back tracked, and installed former finance minister Pravin Gordhan, who calmed the markets, and had just over two months to put together the most important budget, since 1994

Pravin Gordhan Budget speech
I have a simple message from government we are strong enough, resilient enough to overcome our economic challenges

Commentary Four 15 secs
One of the biggest challenges is an imminent downgrade to junk status by the ratings agencies – Moody’s, Standard & Poor’s and Fitch, which means government will pay much more to borrow money. Economist Dawie Roodt explains

Dawie Roodt
if you have a job you better keep it, food will be more expensive, interest rates will go up …its not going to be a nice environment for all of us

LINK
Trevor Manual spent ten long years lifting our credit rating from junk status in 1996 to investment grade in 2006. But here we are back where we began – broke and scrambling for ideas

Commentary five 5sec
Professor Keith Engel was one of the advisors in treasury, under Trevor Manual

Keith
in the 90s we got that under control and we sort lost control of it trying to get the growth and the problem is we put the money in the wrong place instead of putting it in the NDP we put it in the wages – and you put it in the wages its like buying groceries with the credit card and once you do that you are in trouble we spent it on the wages and not on the growth!

Commentary Six 7sec
This year our public service wage bill has ballooned to R469 billion rand

DAWIE ROODT
Something that is very wrong is that we have an army of civil servants and we pay them very handsomely- civil service like wet blanket that is smothering the economy

Commentary Seven 13.5sec
Right now SA is spending more than we earn, and borrowing to make up the difference, so its crucial if the minister is to avoid a downgrade, he must show the ratings agencies we are serious about reducing debt

Minister Pravin Gordhan Budget speech
We cannot borrow beyond our ability to repay. Until we can ignite growth and generate more revenue we have to be tough on ourselves

Commentary eight 8.5sec
So Gordhan is aiming to reduce the deficit from its current 3.9% to 2.4% in 2018

Dawie Roodt
The SA economy is just less than R4 trillion rand, and today the total SA debt is close to R2 trillion rand and interest on two trillion rand is a huge number

LINK
To put that into perspective, consider this – about a third of the income tax we pay goes into servicing just the interest on our public debt – around R130 billion rand a year – that is interest alone and its increasing by around 11 % per annum.

Commentary nine 15.5sec
These are some of the numbers that the ratings agencies consider, especially if the economy isn’t growing – and that is the problem in South Africa – we need at least 3% growth, not the paltry 0.9% we are seeing

Keith
we simply don’t have a growth story here and part of the problem is that it is way beyond the ministers control – secondly are we credible – ok we have a budget that leans strongly I think it will hold up I think the ratings agencies will wait and see and will there be another shock along the way – I think we are in very uncertain territory

Commentary Ten 5sec
Fitch ratings’s Jan Friederich is monitoring SA, from Hong Kong

Jan Friederich
It delivered a significant adjustment of the deficit trajectory / On the downside there are doubts about whether that can actually be achieved – there are questions on whether the GDP growth is sufficiently realistic



Commentary Eleven 9.5sec
Some economists hoped for massive cuts to the civil service, but instead the minister announced a hiring freeze that would save another R25 billion

MINISTER
The expenditure ceiling is cut over the next three years by R25 billion. Mainly by curtailing personnel spending

Commentary Twelve 21 seconds
If you like your fizzy drinks, by April 2017 you will be paying more for those,
Sin taxes are up, you will be spending another 30 cents a litre on petrol, and pay R2.30 per kilogram on new tyres to treasury.

Slight Pause

Economist Trudi Makhaya was pleased that the tax proposals didn’t hurt the middle class or poor

Bongani
We kind of hoped that the minister would pull a rabbit out of the hat but he didn’t do that did he?
Trudi
No he hasn’t he didn’t go for a big bang approach and say lets increase vat or lets increase higher income taxes – there was a very fragmented approach of trying to squeeze out savings and expenditure cuts from many different parts and there is an implementation risk there

Commentary Fourteen 4.5
It’s a concern shared by Fitch Ratings too

Jan Friederich Fitch Ratings
Another question is that it relies on a hiring freeze and it is not entirely certain that will be successfully implemented, and particularly tax measures are not specified and clearly we would be much more comfortable if we knew what measures would be achieving the deficit reduction

Commentary fifteen 6.5
Outside parliament reaction to the budget was mixed, surprisingly the EFF were supportive

Julius
It was a well balanced budget/ he tries to speak to different constituencies that what leadership does

Commentary Sixteen 3.5
But the DA’s David Maynier was disappointed

David Maynier
We expected far deeper expenditure cuts/ the presidents bloated cabinet 74 ministers and deputy ministers – we think could be cut significantly and save up to R4.7 billion per year

Commentary sixteen 3.5 sec
Occasionally the DA and the EFF concur

Julius
If I was a president, I would reduce this useless big cabinet with ministers

Commentary Seventeen 3sec
After his speech, the minister was upbeat

Pravin
I think we have given a message of hope and optimism we have done the right thing, the metrics are looking right we have a growth strategy we have the private sector working with us we are tackling SOE- I believe we are, give us six months and we will begin to see the impact of it

John Webb
you seem a little more optimistic than most people anticipated

Pravin Gordhan
Yay ya, I think people thought we wouldn’t get over the hurdle but we have. I have taken concerns into account and shown once again that SA is capable of meeting those challenges and going beyond

Commentary eighteen 18.5
But then, on Friday, a bombshell. Unbeknown to us the minister was under siege from powerful political forces. A fact he kept silent about for the sake of the country. The Hawks had sent him a letter probing the so called rogue unit at SARS. Was an Invisible power struggle at play?

John
Julius, do you think there is a tension between the office of the treasury and the office of the president

Julius Malema
Well we don’t have the office of the president since it collapsed, and Pravin comes as a Messiah, to come and rescue this country. Zuma has failed and someone said to me you cant say Zuma has failed when Pravin was appointed by Zuma. People forget easily, Pravin was never appointed by Zuma. Pravin was appointed by an intervention process. Zuma till today defends the blunder he made on Van Rooyen.

Commentary nineteen 30.5
To stop the fallout, ANC secretary General Gwede Mantashe weighed in and accused the Hawks of sabotaging the finance minister. Late on Friday Pravin Gordhan released the following statement

“The letter from the Hawks is an attempt by some individuals who have no interest in South Africa, its future, its economic prospects and the welfare of its people. He also said that if necessary he would take appropriate legal action to protect himself and the national treasury

Commentary Twenty 6.5
Gordhan ended his budget speech, with a quote from Nelson Mandela. Now perhaps we understand why

PRAVIN
And I quote – I am fundamentally an optimist whether that comes from nurture or nature I cannot say, part of being optimistic is keeping ones head pointed towards the sun, ones feet moving forward, there are many dark moments when my faith in humanity was sorely tested but I would not and could not give myself up to despair. That way lies defeat and death.

Let’s be resilient. Thank You very much.


THE END

PROMO ONE 15seconds
This week the finance minister juggled the budget to prevent a downgrade to junk status

David Maynier

Julius
It was a well balanced budget/ he tries to speak to different constituencies that what leadership does


PROMO TWO 15seconds
It was the most important budget since 1994 - This week Gordhan delivered his cost cutting budget

John Webb
you seem a little more optimistic than most people anticipated
Pravin Gordhan
Yay ya, I think people thought we wouldn’t get over the hurdle but we have.


PROMO THREE 10 seconder
This week the budget was big news, but on Friday it was overshadowed by political intrigue as a dirty campaign against the finance minister came to light
